utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, July 10, 2008. Let me first greet the witness, the accused, the Defence counsel, as well as Mr. Stringer and his associates, and good morning to everyone assisting us. Today we are going to proceed with the beginning of the cross-examination by the Defence counsel of the other accused. But before we do so, I'm going to read out an oral ruling related to cross-examination of witness Zoran Buntic. At the hearing of the 9th of July, 2008, the Defence teams requested for the cross-examination of the Prlic Defence witness Zoran Buntic the following amount of time: The Defence of accused Stojic requested one hour and a half; the Defence of accused Praljak requested 15 minutes; the Defence of the accused Petkovic asked for about two hours and 15 minutes; the Defence of the accused Coric requested about 45 minutes; and the Defence of the accused Pusic asked for 15 minutes. That's a total of five hours. The Defence teams of Stojic and Petkovic are therefore asking for additional time for their cross-examination. The Trial Chamber would like to note that the Prlic Defence used about seven hours and 15 minutes for its examination-in-chief. Guide-line number 5, paragraph 15, of the decision of the Trial Chamber adopting guide-lines for the presentation of Defence evidence dated 24th of April, 2008, states that the Defence teams conducting a cross-examination will receive 50 per cent of the time used for the direct examination. Furthermore, pursuant to guide-line 5, paragraph 16, of the 24th of April, 2008, decision, the Defence teams should have notified the Chamber of the fact that they wanted to be granted additional time to cross-examine witness Zoran Buntic, and they should have done so in writing and within seven days of the filing of the monthly schedule, indicating which matters they wish to raise with the witness. In view, however, of the examination-in-chief of witness Zoran Buntic, the Trial Chamber agrees on an exceptional basis to consider the late request for additional time submitted by the Stojic and Petkovic Defence teams. After considering the requests submitted by the Defence teams, the Trial Chamber decides by a major, me being in dissent or dissenting, the Trial Chambers decides to grant three hours and 30 minutes to the Defence teams that will lead the cross-examination, and the additional 90 minutes will be deducted from the overall time they were granted to present their case. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber would like to recall that pursuant to guide-line 6, paragraph 20, of the 24th of April, 2008, decision, time spent on matters not raised during the examination-in-chief will be deducted from the time allocated for the presentation of the Defence case of the team conducting the cross-examination. As far as my own dissenting opinion, I have the following reasons. First of all, pursuant to paragraph 16 of guide-line number 6, the Defence teams requesting additional time should have done so in writing and not orally within seven days of the filing of the monthly schedule; and, therefore, as far as I'm concerned, I was not inclined to consider this request and to decide on an exceptional basis to grant the additional time requested. That was my first reason. The second reason I have is that, as far as I'm concerned, the cross-examination conducted by the other accused is only allowable or possible if the other Defence teams have reasons to believe that they can challenge the credibility of the witness or if they believe that the answers the witness provided to the questions put by the other Defence team may incriminate their own client. And I believe that throughout these seven hours and 15 minutes, none of the answers given by the witness to the questions put to him, none of these answers, was likely to incriminate the other accused. Therefore, as far as I'm concerned, there was no ground to grant the three hours and a half for cross-examination purposes. But the Trial Chamber has decided by a majority that the other accused will have three hours and a half to conduct their cross-examination, and that's the way we are going to proceed. Furthermore, the Stojic and Petkovic Defence will have 90 additional minutes. In other words, the other accused will be granted a total of five hours to cross-examine the witness. I don't know who is going to start, but I'm going to give the floor to the first Defence counsel who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Before beginning my cross-examination, I would only like to emphasize two points. As far as the time in extension that I asked for in relation to this witness, I did not ask for a total of two and a half hours. I asked for additional time so that I have just for an hour and a half. That's considerably less than what we said. Second, this concerns that we need to make written submissions requesting additional time within seven days after the schedule is presented. I have to say that based on the witness list, that is, 65 ter (G), we cannot know exactly what's going to be in the direct examination. We can only judge about the contents of the direct examination only after seeing the documents that will be tendered through the witness. We received the definitive list of documents for this witness last Monday morning, and only then were we able to see that some topics will be missing from the direct examination; whereas, some new topics will be discussed through this witness. In any case, we know the definitive contents of the direct examination only once it is over, and only then can we design our cross-examination and assess if we need additional time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just supplement a different point. I'll ask a practical question. It's one we've raised in writing before, and it relates to what Your Honour has just said starting at page 2, line 24, that time spent on matters not raised during examination-in-chief will be deducted from time allocated for the presentation of the Defence case of the team conducting the cross-examination. And it's a certain amount of puzzlement as to exactly how that's going to work. Is that done retrospectively, in which case we're not sure how the computer system does it. It can't be done prospectively on many occasions, because until the evidence has been heard, one can't allocate it into one or other of those boxes. And, also, who and how is that decision made, because essentially, as we have pointed out before, it's a judicial decision; it's not an administrative decision. And the fourth point - I think I've made three points so far - the fourth point would be that, in fairness, we are entitled to know what is being done and to know how the allocation is being done and what allocation is being done, so that we have the opportunity, if necessary, of challenging it. Often it will be very trivial, we acknowledge that; but it could be important on occasions. So not necessarily now, Your Honours, it may be the answer will come from some other source in some other form. But fairly soon, if not now, we would welcome knowing exactly how this procedure is intended to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, the Trial Chamber has duly noted your submissions. I can give you my personal opinion. I fully share what you've just state. It's very difficult, indeed, to decide what is part of the cross-examination and what is part of matters not raised during cross-examination; and as far as I'm concerned, I believe that this can only be decided at the very end because you may have questions asked during cross-examination that are part of cross-examination, but other questions go beyond the scope of cross-examination. You're absolutely right and I fully agree with your concerns, but, obviously, it will be up to the Chamber to rule, after the hearing, how time will be allocated or divided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add something, I would first like to recall that this is not something the Chamber invented, but this is a translation of what is said in Rule 90(H) of the Rules of Procedure. This distinction comes from there. It's not an invention of the Chamber, which also means, if you allow me to finish, that we have practiced it for two years. This applied also, of course, to the Prosecution. We have also applied it after the beginning of the evidence of the Defence, and so far it simply has worked. And I recall that usually the Defence, including Ms. Alaburic, has indicated: I will have these questions that are the same for you, and then I will embark upon a field which does not -- is not the same that was raised in direct. And I am confident that we will be able to apply this as we have done so far without too much difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, the distinction is perfectly clear. We accept that completely; and the distinction that needs to be drawn when counsel is embarking upon cross-examination on matters not raised in examination-in-chief, that's perfectly clear. I was addressing myself to the very real practical problems, and actually underneath them the problems of who makes the decision. The real practical problem is of the actual time allocation which is of real significance in this case given the way that the trial is being managed, and that's actually a separate point, Your Honour, from the clear division. After all, that rule is saying nothing at all about time allocation; it's simply dividing the nature of the cross-examination and the scope of the cross-examination into those two boxes. So, Your Honours, with respect, my question remains on the table and remains requiring an answer, as His Honour, the President, Judge Antonetti, very fairly acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, just one sentence when we have already broached this issue that I believe is very important, but we haven't discussed it before due to very specific circumstances. I believe we have two different rules regarding topics in cross-examination that were not raised in direct. Under the rules of this court, cross-examination is allowed to raise issues that were not broached in direct examination if they are, in a certain way, related to the subject of this trial. As my colleague, Mr. Stewart, said the Rules do not say whether that time goes against the cross-examination time or direct examination time, but the rule on cross-examination says unequivocally that it is the time that belongs to cross-examination. Contrary to that, neither in the guide-lines that the Trial Chamber -- in the guide-lines that the Trial Chamber prepared, we have an opposite rule. The topics raised in cross-examination will go against the time allocated to respective Defences. I would appreciate it very much if the Trial Chamber would consider this comment and change the guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Trial Chamber will clarify all these in due course. I'm going to give the floor now to Mr. Coric's counsel, who is ready. Good morning again, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I asked Mrs. Tomanovic, and I believe she did as I asked and showed you the CD containing registries of various prosecutor's offices, civilian and military, from Mostar, Livno, and Capljina. Before we move to the documents themselves, to facilitate understanding by everyone in the courtroom, I would like us to go through certain abbreviations and acronyms together, those that we'll be able to see both in registries and in documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Chamber has three pages received from us containing these abbreviations and acronyms. It's just an aid, it's not an exhibit. It's just a visual aid. I believe that Mr. Buntic should have a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now read the acronyms and I will just ask the witness to confirm that they, indeed, designate what I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So, on page 1, we see that "K" is a designation for a criminal file, municipal or district; "KT" is a prosecution document; "KTN" is a designation for a prosecution file with a perpetrator unknown; "KTA" is a designation for a prosecution document where it is presumed that no crime has been committed; "KZ" is the acronym for penal code; "ZKP" is the acronym for law on criminal procedure; "KZ RBH" is the penal code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; "KZ SFRY" is the penal code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia; "JT" is the acronym for the public prosecutor; "SUP" is the acronym for the secretariat for internal affairs, later renamed MUP. Mr. Buntic, is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Those are the acronyms that were commonly used to refer to court files and in-court files, and they were also used in everyday speech, documents, textbooks, forms, statistics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let us now turn to page 2 where I listed certain crimes according to the penal code of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Article 36, murder; Article 38, manslaughter; Article 42, serious bodily injuries; Article 55 security breach; Article 56, violation of integrity of an apartment; Article 88, rape; Article 129, illicit trade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Theft.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Article 136 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Article 147, theft.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Article 148, aggravated theft; Article 150 robbery. Article 147, theft; 148, aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 88 is rape. I'm informed by my colleagues that it was not recorded previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Article 150, robbery; Article 153, seizure of motor vehicle; Article 172, inciting a general state of danger; 226, crime of abuse of office or powers. And I singled out one crime, 154, racial and other discrimination from the penal code of the SFRY. Can you confirm all that I said, Mr. Buntic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the first document 5D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, I read the list related to criminal offences with great interest, but it seems to me that there is one article missing, a significant one, the one related to crimes against humanity, war crimes, and so on and so forth. To your knowledge, which article regulated these sorts of crimes, if there was such an article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It existed and it was included in the penal code of the SFRY; that is, the federal penal code. I don't know the exact article, but it is chapter 1 of the federal penal code. There are a number of articles concerning violations of international humanitarian law. I don't know exactly which one this is, but it is a special chapter of the federal penal code.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be assistance of Your Honour, the reason I didn't mention it is that there is chapter 16 of the penal code of the SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The reason I didn't mention it is I wanted to draw some conclusions together with the witness after we look at registries, and then we will talk about how certain crimes were qualified legally and why they were qualified that way. So I wanted to call up into the electronic courtroom 5D 04234.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You have your sets of documents. Could you please find this one. I will try with every document, with every file that we look at, first to show you the documents and then we will try to identify them and compare them to the registry of the prosecutor's office and the number of the prosecution that refers to that case. 5D 04234. It's a criminal report of the police station Capljina, dated 7 July 1993, addressed to the basic public prosecutor's office in Capljina. The number -- the registry number is KT 91/93. This criminal report was filed against a person named Dragan Bunoza. We see that he is an ethnic Croat. The report was filed concerning aggravated theft, Article 148 of the penal code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the injured party is named as Habib Suta. Mr. Buntic, will you agree with me that from the name of the injured party, we see that it is a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, it is a Bosniak, and the report is made against an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Witness. Here we see "KT," but I also see the following: KU 89/93 on the top left corner. What does "KU" stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. KT is a prosecution file. KU, I'm not sure about KU.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, Your Honour. I believe KU concerns internal affairs, and K is crime. I believe it is the police file in which this report is contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just stating the obvious, I take it the Trial Chamber is going to distinguish between the witness's evidence and the representations of counsel, which may be correct and I'm not disputing them. But I think that we don't really know what KU is in an official way until a witness has said what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you confirm what the Defence counsel has just explained, or is it something you really can't tell us anything about? Would KU mean that this is a document coming from the civilian police and that it was thus recorded here or registered here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by my previous answer. I'm not sure, so I cannot affirmatively state whether it is or isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at PD 04246 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel kindly adjust her microphone. We have trouble hearing her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find these documents. I don't know whether I've been given these documents, and I don't know in which order they were given to me or should I follow them on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You should have it on the screen. We handed them over to the court deputy, and I think that you should have all the documents. Is there any way the court deputy can help you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which order they are registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. The usher, who's very experienced, is going to help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear that it says "PD" in the transcript, and it should say "5D," 5D.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters again kindly ask that counsel adjust her microphone. We have great trouble hearing her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we have a problem. Perhaps I can give the witness my own copy where all the documents are put in the right order, but you can see it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: What really matters for me are names and numbers. We have here a document of the higher prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the number, there is too much background noise, and we cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't know, I think only a few of us are listening in the English; but on the English channel we're hearing from the booth that they're asking counsel to adjust her microphone, so that they can hear her more clearly because they're having trouble hearing counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have been the culprit because my microphone was still on. I may be the one responsible for it, and she's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So what we have here is a document of the higher prosecutor's office in Mostar. Later on, we are going to look at the basic prosecutor's documents and the higher prosecutor's number. KT 44/93 is the number. Yet, again, it has to do with a crime for Article 148. We see that the defendants are the same; and further on in the text, in the very last paragraph on the first page, we can all see the name of the injured party, again as Habib Suta. I think it is obvious that it is the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now I'm not going to read this out, but everyone in the courtroom can read the entire document and see that the crime described is the same, and this is a motion to issue an indictment without conducting an investigation. Later on -- or rather, we should move to the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me ask you a technical question which may be of relevance to the Trial Chamber when we look into the issue of Article 7(3) of the Statute. Through this case, we saw that there is a police report sent to the prosecutor. The prosecutor seizes the investigative judge of the file; that is, the judge in Mostar. Let us imagine that the judges would do nothing or that he would say that no crime was committed. The judge does nothing or just keeps the file in a file of documents. Can the prosecutor appeal if a judge fails to do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prosecutor always had such possibilities; that is to say, to call for an investigation to be carried out and to seek information about the investigation. Also, if the investigating judge believes that there are no elements for issuing an indictment, the prosecutor can file an appeal against that decision to a panel of judges. So the prosecutor does have all these possibilities available even after the investigation was carried out. Obviously, this is a document of the deputy senior prosecutor. I know that this was Mr. Blago Dodig, and it is his document. Again, I see on the basis of the designator in this document, again we see that this is a KT document; that is to say, a prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this very clear explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we have document 5D 04151.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's going to appear on the screens. Don't bother trying to find it. 5D 04246 -- or rather, 4151. I am going to say that it is the indictment that was issued by the senior public prosecutor's office in Mostar. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the next document in relation to this; that is, 5D 04236.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now we see the judgement that was passed by the high court in Mostar, and the number is K 18/94. Can you confirm to me that this K 18/94 designates a court file, and since it says 1994 that the prosecutor handed over these files to the high court in Mostar in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, on the basis of the designator, because this is -- it is a court file. As for the names of the accused persons, it is obvious that this is the same case that we've been following through all the time, through all the stages, from filing a report and then issuing an indictment and then passing a judgement. It is obvious on the basis of the number of the file and the names of the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see in e-court 2112 from 5D 04288.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a KT register of the senior prosecutor's office in Mostar. Here it is. I think that in the third box we see -- or rather, before we look at it, Mr. Buntic, will you agree with me that the prosecutor's list contains the number of the file, the name of the accused, the name of the person filing the charges, and the name of the injured party inter alia? It contains other elements, too, but this is what matters the most for us at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just seen it on my screen, so I need to have a look. Yes, that is the information concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We can all see that in the fourth column we find the names of the accused, and two columns onwards we see the name of the injured person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In the first rubric, we see KT 44, and that is that number KT 44/93 that we saw earlier on in the documents of the senior prosecutor's office in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2317, please. Here it is. Column 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's the first number we looked at of the prosecutor's office in Mostar, KT 91/93. Can you confirm that it is one and the same case and that is the number?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the names that appear on the screen, it is obvious that it is the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D 04245 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Unfortunately, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, we have not received this document in paper. We just -- what we have here is a photocopy of a CD which is not, in fact, very helpful. Now, could we see this again, Usher, and see it all to the end of the form because we have only the left part, and obviously the form is bigger. What is on -- I would like to see what follows, whether there is any other entry on the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that it can be moved left and right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see the entire procedure. I do apologise to the Trial Chamber, but quite simply there is no photocopier that is big enough, either in this Tribunal or the court in Mostar. I believe that some specialised institutions for photocopying perhaps may have such facilities; but, technically, in our investigation, we could not make a hard copy of this document for technical reasons. That is why we provided the CD in the 65 ter list; and, again, we provided it at an early stage so that everyone could become aware of it. I do apologise. But for technical reasons, there was no other way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I take that. Architecture offices normally have big photocopying machines because they use them for plans and that might be where you could find assistance, but I'm glad that this was possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- one moment. I have a question for the witness. At some point in time, you were in charge of the justice area. We have this document in front of us; and as was pointed out by counsel just now, we can see that this entire case was recorded in the office of the prosecutor. And for those like me who know how justice works, how the judiciary works, we can see that this entire case is recorded in this type of registry or register. The prosecutor, whomever he may be, when he or she receives a case from the police, were they obliged to record everything in a register, mentioning every step of the proceedings including the final decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Once a criminal report is received, that is to say, when a prosecutor receives it from the police, he is duty-bound to record the criminal report in his own records. As the colleague already mentioned, it has to do with prosecution registers that are of large format. That is what they looked like. It is true that this is a standard form that was used in the former Yugoslavia as well. This is not a new form at all and the format, too, is standard, like the ones that existed before the war. And the prosecutor's office kept the file once they received it from the police or from the citizen concerned or from authorised officials. And then, as we can see here, from beginning to end, they're going to keep it in their own register. The court also keeps it in its own register once they receive it, and then they keep it up until the end. As you know, it can go from first instance to second instance even to third-instance courts, and then it receives different designation numbers from each and every one of the courts involved and in connection with the legal remedies that were involved in terms of the decisions of the lower courts. You see here that the file was recorded by the prosecutor's office and it's one and the same file. It's obvious here from the numbers, designators, as well as the names of the accused persons and the name of the injured party. It is one and the same file or case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 5D 04245.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting to see it on our screens - here it is - yet again this is a special report of the Capljina police station sent to the senior public prosecutor's office. Again, we see the KT 74/93 number, as it was received in the prosecutor's office. We see from the document - we can have a look - that the crime involved is aggravated theft from Article 148 and the suspect is Andrej Zovko. It says that he's an ethnic Croat, a national of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And Adem Fazlagic is the injured party. Sir, can we agree yet again on the basis of the names that the accused person is an ethnic Croat and the injured party an ethnic Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This special report itself says that the -- a person charged is an ethnic Croat and the injured party is an ethnic Bosniak. We can see it by the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: One more thing in relation to this that is of interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look underneath the name in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says that the person was suspected of committing other crimes, falsifying documents and false representation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 2 now, and the paragraph that starts with the words: "On the 19th of May ..." I don't want to read the entire paragraph because we can all read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The person misrepresented himself impersonating a police officer and he falsified a police ID, forged a police ID. Sir, do you know that there were cases when different perpetrators of crimes falsely represented themselves as members of the police or the military; whereas, they were not members of either?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of such cases. For the most part, it had to do with persons who had had a criminal record. They were trying to take advantage of the war situation and the fact that all state organs were functioning with difficulty. So they tried to take advantage of the situation, and we can see that they used it for looting, theft, and different forms of property-related crime. So the times did make it easier for such people to engage in crime. This is not an isolated case; there were other such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: When we were looking at page 1 of this document, we saw that below the heading "Special Report," there's another line supplementing the criminal report. On page 3 in -- page 4 in English and page 3 in Croatian, we see the relevant information. From the brief description of crime following the word "because," we see that the crime is against Adem Fazlagic and that it is the same offence described in the supplement to the criminal report. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is obviously the same case and the same persons, both the injured party and the offender, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Under the rubric "against," we see NN. Does that mean that at the time of the report, the perpetrator was unknown and his name was given only in the supplement to the criminal report? Does that mean that the investigation resulted in an identification of the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A criminal report against perpetrator NN means unknown perpetrator. So it is the same person, Adem Fazlagic, as we have seen before from these documents shown earlier. And from the later procedure, we see that it is the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While we are with the unknown perpetrator, do you know that a special problem for prosecuting authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. The last number of a document that I find in the record is 5D 04245. I guess that you have switched to another document, but I missed the number and it is not recorded. You're on the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same document, Your Honour. It's just page 4, the same document, page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you know that for the prosecution authorities and the judiciary, the group of unknown perpetrators were a special problem, and can you say something about this phenomenon, why was it able to occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, I think if a person just walked into the courtroom or the gallery, they would assume that they're watching a direct examination because that's really what's happening here. I think we need to be honest about what the status of this investigation is. It's only different from a real direct examination by the fact that these documents were provided to the Prosecutor yesterday and that, of course, we've received no summary or prior indication of the nature or the scope of this direct examination. So it's certainly not a direct examination in that respect. But I am going to object to the use of leading questions. I've been hesitant to do so. I think it's fair to let counsel lead to the extent necessary and it moves things along faster to allow us to navigate through these documents, particularly through these photocopies. But at the same time, this is a direct examination. I think leading questions, such as the one that's being put to the witness now, are inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Counsel, try to take into account what the Prosecutor has just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us anything about the criminal prosecution of unknown perpetrators? Did such a problem exist and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a recurring problem, a constant problem. It's better perhaps to explain using an example. For instance, at a location known as Ubarak, around 70 bodies were discovered, and it was presumed they resulted from a crime committed by the Yugoslav Army before they withdrew from Mostar. After the discovery of these bodies, normally a criminal report was filed recording this crime, but even that report was filed naming unknown perpetrators, referring to unknown perpetrators, because neither the civilian police nor the military police nor the prosecutor had access to information about the persons who might have committed it and there existed another problem. Even if they had been able to file a criminal report against specific persons, those persons had by that time become inaccessible. They had left the territory together with the Yugoslav Army; and even if one were able to identify a perpetrator to the degree of well-grounded suspicion, as the phrase goes, there was this other problem. And at this time, there were, indeed, a number of similar problems that made the work of the prosecutors and the judiciary difficult. Not only in this case but in many cases criminal reports were filed against perpetrators unknown, but this is a very eloquent example of the whole category.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 5D 04153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since counsel has finished examining the document, I'd like to go back to it for a detail. I looked at it closely. I was interested in it, and I see that the author of these offences, there are many of them, hails from Mostar. He went to Capljina, and he wore a camouflage uniform and green beret and was armed with a rifle. At the time, as far as you know because you were in the area, was it customary to see individuals circulating, moving around, in camouflage gear with green or red berets and armed individuals? Was it something normal, current?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I do have an example that might be illustrative. After the 4th of April, 1993 [as interpreted], there were international monitors in Citluk, five of them; and on a daily basis or once every two days, they called on the command of the Citluk Battalion. And they asked me, and it was typical for their whole stay in that area of two or three months, they asked me how come they never saw a person in civilian clothes. For the duration of their stay, they did not see a person in civilian, a woman, a child, or an elderly person. All persons who were not fit for the army were by that time removed from Citluk, and everyone was moving around wearing military uniforms. Sometimes it was the uniform of people serving in the civilian protection, sometimes it was a police uniform, but it was always a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The witness said that it was the period after 4th April 1993, and it was recorded -- I believe that it must be 1992 because that's the year when the witness was in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether I made a slip of the tongue or it was recorded inaccurately. I thought I said 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, do you have some knowledge in criminology, statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed yesterday a large number of reports that misdemeanour courts filed, civilian courts filed, prosecutor's offices filed. A large number of reports went into evidence, and they contain all sorts of statistics about cases dealt with by prosecution offices and tried in various courts. You will see that there are thousands of cases there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, are you also aware of studies that establish the percentage of crimes where an author is eventually found, as compared to those where the author remains unknown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From statistics, I can agree that the ratio between detected, charged, and convicted persons is considerably lower in this period and the statistics in peacetime. So, in this period, much fewer perpetrators were detected and tried than in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you have any figures that established this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in principle, I'm talking about pre-war statistics at the level of Yugoslavia. The number of elucidated cases and identified perpetrators was 75 to 80 per cent, and the number of convictions compared to the number of indictments was also around 70 per cent. And I believe it is quite understandable, and it is not even to be expected, that in times of war when armies came and went and one war was immediately followed by another and the buildings of courts were completely destroyed and the number of judges, as you saw on the example of the municipal court in Mostar, 10 out of 23 judges left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. I did not actually ask for interpretation and so forth. What I would finally also like to know is whether you are aware or whether you have compared these figures with the figures of other countries? And, of course, the average is one thing, but normally the investigations differentiate between different kinds of crimes and the elucidation rate differs also very much as to the kind of crime. What you have told us has sounded very familiar to me. I also had to do with the criminal prosecutions, where quite a considerable number of offence could not be elucidated, no author was ever found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we had the possibility to compare. I don't think it was possible to compare that with another state in a state of war. We could only compare with the statistics maintained by other countries and that Yugoslavia, too, had maintained in other peacetime conditions. But I'm not aware that anyone in those wins of war could reliably keep such statistics about the number of committed crimes, identified versus unknown perpetrators, and the number of convictions. I don't know that such statistics exist, and I don't think I could have used them for comparison. I could only compare to peacetime. But in the state of war, and as I said one war was immediately followed by another, the comparative method was not of much use to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I would like to follow-up on what His Honour Judge Trechsel said concerning statistics and the possibility to prosecute. We heard yesterday from you about the shortage of judges, and we saw the example of the engineer who was misdemeanour magistrate. We saw that in your reports. But what can you tell us about forensic experts, ballistic experts, medical forensic experts, and other experts that are indispensable for prosecuting the gravest crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ballistic experts, we did not have any in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We did not have a single forensic expert. We had some medical experts, but we did have a single graphologist in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And in those circumstances, we had no other choice but to ask someone from the Republic of Croatia to come over because we had no physical communication with other parts of the country, and it was impossible to establish such communication. And the only thing we could do is address a request either to an institution or to an expert personally in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 5D 04153.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's the last document concerning this case before we move on to the register. We see from the document that it is a decision of the higher court in Mostar. Look at the name of the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And the name of the injured party on page 2. Can you confirm that it is the same person we discussed before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see page 1. I can see that it is a court file by the designation K. I see that the accused -- the defendant is an ethnic Croat. I just got page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 1, para 1, and you will see the name of the injured party. You will see it now. In English, we have the right page. Look at the sentence beginning: "On 17th May 1992 ..." and then read the name of the injured party.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it's the person we discussed before, Mr. Adem Fazlagic, and the defendant is Andrej Zovko.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court image 2313. It is part of the KT register of the prosecutor's office in Capljina. Here it is, the one-but-last.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You can have a look at all of it. Once you've had a look, can you confirm that it's the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously, this is a copy of the prosecutor's register, and, obviously, it's the same case, judging by the names of the persons involved, namely, the accused and the injured party, and also the numbers under which they were filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to 5D 303482 -- P 03482.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, while everybody's looking for it, I will say that this is a document of the department for fighting crime at the military police administration in Mostar dated the 16th of July, 1993. It is the record of an interview of a member of the military police. In the record of interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really have to read it out, everyone can see it in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, there is a reference to three persons in addition to the person being interviewed; namely, three persons who are members of the military police. And in the second paragraph, in order to protect the identity of the person involved, I'm not going to mention the names, it would be rather indelicate of me. The injured parties are two persons of the female gender. Sir, please don't give us the names, but tell me, at least as far as one of these female persons is concerned, can we on the basis of her name conclude that she's an ethnic Bosniak, or rather, Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is with a high degree of probability that that conclusion can be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P 03571 is the next document. Could we all please look at page 2 of the document first. P 03571. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a request of the military police sent to the military police administration on the 18th of July, 1993. We see from this request that what is requested is that four military policemen be removed from duty because they had committed the crime of rape as well as gross breaches of military discipline. Can we confirm that it is evident that these are the same persons from the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the first page of this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It is an authorisation issued by the chief of administration of the military police, Valentin Coric, dated the 19th of July, 1993. This is an authorisation to remove from duty those policemen whose names we've already seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. But at page 30, line 2, the answer of the witness hasn't been properly or fully recorded at this moment. Perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I not right if I say that earlier on you confirmed to me that the four names were the four names mentioned in the previous document, that these were the same four military policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I confirmed in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So now I said that we have an authorisation here, and it states inter alia what I have already stated. And it also says that these persons tarnished the name of the military police, that their further presence in this unit would be detrimental, and that the entire case was submitted to the military prosecutor's office. Sir, you are familiar with military discipline rules. Is this the right kind of procedure that is to be taken in such a case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this indicates that there was consistent implementation of the rules on military police discipline, and also these persons were removed from police duty and criminal proceedings were instituted against them. So I see that this authorisation moves in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I would like us to look at 2413 and 2414 of the KT register of the municipal prosecutor's office in Mostar. Would you please look at the last column; the first one is 2413. I would be interested in the first rubric. In it we see VT Mostar KT 265/93. Can you confirm that this means that the case was transferred to the municipal prosecutor's office in Mostar from the military prosecutor's office, and that in the military prosecutor's office, it was registered under number KT 265/93?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VT Mostar would mean military prosecutor's office; whereas, KT obviously shows that it's a prosecutor's file. The rest is the number of the file.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at the second column. Could we scroll up a bit so that we see the top of this column, so that we see what it says. Further on, further on. Yes. Could you zoom it in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is the column where the persons against whom proceedings are instituted are recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: No. I am asking about the previous column because I think that that has to do with the authority that is actually bringing the charges, but we can't really see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back down again.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see that it says VP in the next column. Is VP an abbreviation for the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VP, yes, military police; whereas, VT is military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say for the record, if anyone challenges this, I would like to ask the Prosecutor to check what I'm saying now, but we don't really have much time now. We don't have the technical facilities, but I think that the column says, at the top, that this is who is bringing the criminal charges against someone so that can be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: If we're looking at these names, let us look at the fourth column and all the rest that is stated here. Is it not obvious that this is one of the persons whose names we saw in the previous documents of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2414, could we see that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's the same number. This is the way it's been dealt with technically. Please look at the names of the first three persons on the list and the column of the injured party. So are these the remaining three?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. Judging by the names, these are the three remaining persons who appeared in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say for the record that there is image 1828 that I'm not going to call up now. That is registry of the district prosecutor's office in Mostar. The number is KT 265/93, and that is how it was filed. We can see on the basis of this register that I showed that it was a case that was transferred on the basis of both numbers. Could we please have a look at PD 04172 [as interpreted] -- 5D. 5D 04172. Have we found it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This has to do with a criminal complaint of the military police of Mostar, dated the 16th of June, 1992, against Jelenko Brajkovic for having stolen a motor vehicle. And in the description of the crime concerned, we see that it is an automobile that was owned by Rent-A-Car Sarajevo. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to show a short set of documents in relation to this. 5D 04171.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While the document is being searched, I will say that this is a document of the district military prosecutor's office in Mostar. Let us remember the number, KT 40/92; and the date is the 5th of January, 1993. This is a request to conduct an investigation sent to the district military court in Mostar to the investigating judge. Tell us, sir, when we look at this request and the name of the accused person and the name of the injured party, is it one and the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the KT number, 40/92, it is obvious that it is a prosecutor's file. It is obvious from the request itself that it involves the persons that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D 04170, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the district military court in Mostar, KI 90/93. This is a ruling on conducting an investigation, dated the 9th of April, 1993. Now I have a few questions in relation to this document. Tell us, KI, that is an investigative file, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A court investigative file; that is to say, in the investigations stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see the name and surname of the judge down here. Is the judge an ethnic Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an investigating judge of the then-court in Mostar. I know him personally, Husnija Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the information about the suspect and the injured party, is it one and the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jelenko Brajkovic, the suspect we already discussed. And the company concerned is the Rent-A-Car company, and I can confirm that it is the case you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we display 1627, KT register of the district court in Mostar. We have that KT number, 40/92. Yes, here it is; the first person, the first column.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the information there. Here, it is more legible. You see what it says here: "Who is bringing the charges" and the rest. Can you confirm that it's the -- it's one and the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask how much time I have left so that I see what else I'm going to show as far as these documents are concerned. I don't know whether I'll have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has just told me that you've used 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have a break now so that I can organize my documents? I would just like to say that the Trial Chamber that I have some documents that are extremely important. This is a document against a member of security in Dretelj. It has to do with the theft of money, and also a few other important things like attack against civilians of Bosniak ethnicity in Mostar, a typical case. And we've heard about such things in this courtroom. I would like to go through these documents because I believe that would be in everyone's interest; and, finally, I don't mind having it taken away from my time ultimately because all of this is moving far slower than I thought it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had been granted 45 minutes by a decision taken by the Trial Chamber by a majority. You've used these 45 minutes. Now you may use additional time if you like, but it will be deducted from your overall time. So it's not a problem. We'll have a 20-minute break because in any case the time had come to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. Registrar, let me give you the floor because you have two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, actually it's a rectification of the two IC numbers that were given yesterday. The first map referring to the district of Mostar shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00825, and the second map referring to Livno shall be given Exhibit Number IC 00826, instead of 826 and 827, as referred to in the record yesterday. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You may proceed, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. During the break, we produced two copies -- before the break, we dealt with -- before the break, we dealt with two examples, and now I'd like to call up 5D 04164. The reason I'm asking for this document, apart from comparing it with the register, is that it will answer the question of the President concerning the abandonment of criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Here, we have the document. It's a criminal report of the crime prevention department from the military police administration, Mostar division, dated 22 July 1993, filed against Stanko Zelenika. We see in the personal details of this person that it was a member of the 2nd Brigade. He is charged with aggravated robbery, aggravated theft. The report was filed under number KT 5/93. Can you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I call up now 5D 04179.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a request to conduct an investigation filed to the district military court. We see the same number, KT 588/93; and on the stamp of receipt of the military court, it was filed under KI 118/93. Can you agree that it's the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see before me is a document under number KT 588/93. I don't think -- I'm not sure. Is that the same document? It's a request to conduct an investigation, correct, but what I see on the screen is the document of the district military prosecutor's office in Mostar on the 3rd August 1993 under number KT 588/93.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct. And then the second number that I mentioned of the military court written in hand is on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the third paragraph starting with the words: "Perpetrated the criminal offence from Article 150 ..." And can we now look at the last page, it's also in the second page, points 1, 2, and 3. Under point 2, we see the names of persons who need to be interviewed as witnesses in the case. Turn to page 2 so that the gentleman can see it. We see the English, and now we see the Croatian as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the persons in item 2, Hadzo Brkic and Hidzad Hadziomerovic, are they Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the names, it is very likely that they are Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 5D 04178. It's a decision to conduct an investigation from the district military court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We have that number KI that was handwritten on the previous document, KI 118/93. Can you confirm it's the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, it is a document of the district military prosecutor's office. It's a case in the phase of investigation, KI 118/93; and, obviously, it is about the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 5D 04175. This is a document with the same number, KI 118/93, document of the district military court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a decision, a ruling, terminating investigation against the accused. And the second paragraph after the word "ruling" is what my colleague Ms. Nozica emphasized in response to the question by President Antonetti. It says: "The injured party may within eight days of receiving notification continue the criminal prosecution of the accused by submitting a request doctor facial investigation or filing an indictment." And then we have a sentence stating that appeal is allowed before the appeals chamber. First of all, tell me, do you think it is about the same case; and, second, is this an example of abandoning the charges? That's the question asked earlier by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the number of this file, KI 118/93, and from the text of this ruling, it is obvious that it is the same case. That's the answer to your first question. And, second, item 2 of this ruling indicates the legal right of the injured party that in case of termination of prosecution, he can continue the prosecution himself by submitting a request for additional investigation or by raising an indictment. Those were the two legal possibilities at the disposal of the injured party. We see from the body of the ruling, I believe that it was taken according to the law prevailing then.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little to see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In English, it's obviously on page 2; but in Croatian, you can see in the left bottom corner, legal relief, legal recourse.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. It is the right that I just described, and the appeal should be lodged with the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought Judge Trechsel had a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, at least before you leave the document, but I don't want to interrupt unnecessarily and prematurely. Are you done? Then I would like to refer to the last paragraph on the English page which should be rolled down. Up again a little bit or down. Yes, the last paragraph. This is a paragraph giving the reasons for the decision not to prosecute, and it is not a substantive reasoning given here but a referral to the decision of the public prosecutor. It was a public prosecutor who decided not to proceed, and the judge seems to be rubber-stamping this, which may be perfectly all right, I'm not criticising. But, Mr. Buntic, somewhere are there reasons for the decision? Can the victim know why the decision not to prosecute was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you probably -- I mean, you probably know what I know. To comment on the legality of a judicial decision is very difficult. It's difficult to comment on the reasons. Its legality is hinged on the legal remedies, and the second-instance court decides on it. If the higher instance finds that the statement of reasons is not well explained or well grounded, then it would be a violation of the appeals procedure. Therefore, if the injured party considers that the reasons given are not clear enough or that they are contrary to the ruling, then it would be a violation of the criminal -- it would be a violation of the proceedings -- of due process. And in that case, he would file an appeal and the appeal would be decided by the appeals chamber, by a higher-instance court, composed of three judges. So the party does have a legal recourse, or take over the prosecution himself or herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have told us that. I reiterate, I'm not criticising. I'm just trying to get all the facts, and let me put it in another way or slightly different questions. Did the victim in this case normally have a copy of the decision of the public prosecutor's office not to prosecute; and if so, would that decision contain a short summary of what was attempted with the resultant reasons why no prospect is seen in going on with the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, that's how I read this statement of reasons, is that it does not deviate from standard statements of reason given in similar cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance to Judge Trechsel, can you tell me, sir, do you know if the injured party had to have the right to seek information from the prosecutor and be informed of the file?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear enough. His legal recourse -- his right to legal recourse starts only from the day when the ruling is made, and there is a dead-line of three days from receipt of the ruling and that is the time within which he had the right to file a request for additional investigation or take the prosecution upon himself through a lawyer or himself. Those were the two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at image 1869, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe just a small point. You have said or it is recorded here that there was a dead-line of three days from receipt of the ruling for further steps to be taken by the victim; whereas, in the document before us, the second paragraph of the part entitled "Ruling" speaks of a time-limit of "within eight days." Was it a slip of the tongue of yours when you said three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not a slip of the tongue. He could lodge an appeal within three days, and within eight days he could start a prosecution himself by bringing an indictment or filing a request for additional investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for image 1869. It's an extract from the KT register of the district military court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see somewhere towards the middle of the screen the name of the person. In the second -- it's, in fact, the fourth column that the filing party is the administration in Mostar and the defendant is Stanko Zelenika. Do you agree it's the same person we've discussed before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see the information from the second and fourth columns. From the first column, we see that it's the administration of the military police that files the report, and the defendant is, indeed, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D 04194, please. It's a request to carry out an investigation from the district military prosecutor's office in Mostar, number KT 1033/93, dated 22 August 1993. 5D 04196. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see the name of the defendant under para 1 and para 2 on page 1. We see the names of the injured parties. Are they Bosniaks? We see a few members of the Becirevic family and a few members of the Kajtaz family.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these last names, I can say with a high degree of probability that they are Muslims, Bosniaks. As for the name and surname of the person against whom this request was filed, I can also say with a great degree of probability that it is an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display page 2 now, and could we all pay attention to the paragraph above the words: "I propose."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see here that it has to do with a crime of murder and the crime of rape. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to the next document now, 5D 04215.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the district military court in Mostar. The number is KI 122/93, dated the 23rd of August, 1993. This is a decision to open an investigation. As we look at this document, sir, can we agree that it is a decision that was made on the basis of the request that was the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that on the basis of the number of the file and the names of the persons that this decision pertains to. It is obvious that it is the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I think that this is going to be an answer to His Honour Judge Trechsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 5D 0461 -- 4160, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the district military prosecutor's office, and it is dated the 15th of October, 1993, and the KT number is 1033/93, and it is entitled "Official Note." In the first sentence of this document, it is stated that: "Upon completing the investigation against Vedran Bijuk, the decision is made not to pursue the matter further due to lack of evidence." In the next two paragraphs, the reasons for this are stated; and in the last sentence it is stated, I quote: "Because of the above, I have decided not to proceed with criminal prosecution of the accused Vedran Bijuk." Can we agree that it is the same case, and the same proceedings, the same names that we showed in the previous documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. There is a small problem. This is a public document. The name of an individual is mentioned therein. Maybe this person was a victim of a crime. I'm going to ask the registrar to redact this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, yes, it's not been broadcast outside this courtroom. That's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I repeat the question. Do you agree with me that it is one and the same case in relation to the previous documents that we showed about the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the name of the person against whom this investigation was initiated and also in respect of the injured parties' names, obviously it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1957, please. Again, this is an extract from the Mostar office. Let us just have this enlarged. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The third one from the top, we see again it is the military police administration. Bijuk Vedran, nickname Splico, that's the name of the accused. Can we agree that it is precisely the records of the case that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, it's one and the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now move on to document 5D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a technical question. Regarding this case, Bijuk, I noted that in the original document for the criminal report we have his name, it is indicated that he is from the Republic of Croatia. But curiously enough his military unit is not mentioned; however, it is the military prosecutor that is now here prosecuting. Normally he prosecutes somebody who is a military, a serviceman; otherwise, it would be a civilian prosecutor. Why is the military unit not mentioned? Do you have an explanation for that in case you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like here, the court or the prosecutor, when initiating proceedings, takes personal details. And I think that we saw from the previous documents that the name and surname and date of birth are registered, as well as the address and nationality of the persons involved. In everyday court practice, the name of the unit was recorded as well. Since this is a military court and the district military prosecutor, I think that the name of the unit should have been referred to as well, the name of the unit that he belonged to. However, I see that it is not designated. I cannot go into the reasons for that. I would engage in speculation, or rather, guess-work which I think would not -- would not be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 5D 04248. This is a criminal report. I do apologise, but I'm afraid that the honourable President of the Trial Chamber hasn't switched off his microphone. Now it is fine. I heard it in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry. I had turned it off. I'm not the culprit this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
