utterances.text: We have a criminal report of the crime prevention department of the military police administration Mostar section. The 19th of August, 1993, is the date. It was submitted to the military -- district military prosecutor in Mostar. We have the delivery stamp that it was received; that is, KT 1116/93 is there as the number. We also see the date. We see that the criminal report was filed against a person by the name of Milenko Kordic, a member of the HVO, and the crime involved is murder. I would like us to look at page 3 of this document. This is an attachment accompanying this criminal report, and it has to do with a statement of a person in relation to this case. Could we please remember this. I have a reason for showing this. In the second paragraph, this person says that the suspect told her that he took some Muslims out, killed them, and threw them into the Neretva River. Please remember this sentence before we move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to call up document 5D 04255.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Again, this is a documents of the military police administration sent to the district military court in Mostar. It's dated the 24th of August, 1993, and we see the stamp showing that it was received and we see that an official note is being enclosed with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see the official note if we look at the next page, so could that be done, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says here that the military police officer in charge came to realize that the suspect took out and killed a person of Muslim ethnicity. We see that from the text. Sir, am I right if I conclude that in this case the military police, after having handed over the case to the military prosecutor, since it obtained new knowledge, they provided this additional knowledge in terms of the possible crimes that this person had committed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the text of this official note, it is obvious that this is in addition to the already filed criminal report, after new knowledge was gained after the criminal report had been filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at document 5D 04247.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It is an indictment of the district prosecutor's office in Mostar. The KT number is 1116/93. The date is the 27th of September, 1993. We see in the upper right-hand corner the stamp of the district military court in Mostar, showing that the document had been received. On the basis of the name and the date, can we conclude that it is one and the same case and that it has to do with the documents that we have seen previously?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The number of the file, both in the court and in the prosecutor's office, and the names of the persons involved or charged. It is obvious that it's the same case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show 1965. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We can see somewhere around the middle of the screen, the military police administration is Milenko Kordic. Do you agree with me that that is a record of this case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to the next document, 5D 04181.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Again, it is a criminal report, this time of the Capljina division; and the date is the 7th of September, 1993. The criminal complaint is being filed against Veselko Kozina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we all have a look at the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see here that the criminal complaint is filed against Veselko Kozina; and in the statement of reasons, we see that the crime involved relates to Article 226 and that is overstepping authority. And we see that in both cases it had to do with taking money away from detainees in Dretelj, with the cooperation of a detainee named Trebinjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I highlight the name because we heard the name several times during the Prosecution case, and I think that everyone in this courtroom is familiar with it. Could we now look at document 5D 04182.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a request to carry out an investigation, and the number is KT 1556/93. The date is the 24th of September, 1993, and this is being filed with the district military court in Mostar. Sir, as we look at this document, can you agree with me that it is one and the same case in terms of the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the name of the person against whom the investigation is required, we see that it is the same case and it has reached the second stage; namely, this is a request for investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 2010. We see it now, the name. Can we scroll down a little because we need to see that the filing party is the same. So we need to see who it was filed by, the military police of Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And when we look lower down, we see the name of the accused. Do we agree that this is the record of the case at the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see from the name of the person filing the report and the name of the accused that it's the same case, and from the personal details.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to 5D 04183.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a document of the higher public prosecutor's office in Mostar -- in fact, a document of the district military prosecutor's office sent to the higher public prosecutor's office. Number is KT 2789/93, and the date is 9 December 1993. We see the number under which it was received, KT 57/93, received on the same day. Let us clarify this. The higher public prosecutor's office is a civilian prosecution office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The suspect -- in fact, the accused is Bozidar Skobic and the crime is robbery. And in paragraph 2, we see the reason why this case is deferred; namely, that the accused is relieved of compulsory military duty in view of his sickness. Can you confirm that in this case the civilian court is competent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the statement of reasons, we see that this person is relieved of military duty, which means demobilised, and turned into a civilian. So the military prosecutor's office and the district military court are no longer in charge; it is the civilian courts and civilian prosecutors who are in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 both in English and this Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In the description of the offence, we see the name of one more person. Do you agree it is a Bosniak person who is the injured party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a high degree of probability.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at image 1223. It is, again, the register of the district military prosecutor's office, report filed by the military police, and the name of the person is Bozidar Skobic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you identify this as the same case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, yes. We can see that from the name of the person and his personal details.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We'll now deal with the last example regarding the register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Buntic, you have said that one of the persons mentioned on page 3 of this document was of Muslim ethnicity, or religion, rather, actually. Could you identify which name you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said with a high degree of probability. It's impossible to be 100 per cent sure. But judging by the name of the person that I saw on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Which name? Which name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I no longer see it on the screen. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the previous page, 5D 04183. There are three names. You had the third page a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the name was Sadi.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Is that the name in line 4?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think what is written here as "Saji" is wrong; it's probably "Sadi." I think Saji could be wrong possibly. But in both cases, whichever it is, Saji, Sadi, I said with a high degree of probability it's a Bosniak. It's not advisable to state something with a hundred per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would that also be deduced from the family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the family name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saji could be also Saja. The family name does not sound Bosniak, but the first name could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P 07846.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed, let me tell you that you've already used 30 additional minutes on top of the 45 minutes initially granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm aware of that. But I believe this is important, and I don't mind if it is deducted from my time later. I think we are actually saving time by dealing with this. Let's move on to the next document regarding registers, P 07846. We have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's a criminal report of the 1st Military Police Battalion, crime prevention military police, sent to the military state prosecutor in Mostar concerning a person named Zeljko Silic. What is of interest to me in this document is on page 2. We have the legal qualification of criminal acts charged at this person: The crime of causing public danger. We see that the accused had entered the apartment of the injured party, Tidza Hadrovic, and set certain items on fire. Do you agree that this is again a Bosniak injured party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would have to state that it is so with a high degree of probability, judging by both the first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The second crime is racial and other discrimination. We see that it is governed by Article 154 in the penal code of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We see the name of the street, that the used mistreated occupants of the residential building in that street, driven them out from their apartments, addressed slurs to them, insulted them, and threatened. When you spoke about this article of the penal code of the SFRY, did you mean this crime as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The third crime is security breach pursuant to Article 55 of the law of -- of the penal code of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same accused threatening the life and limb of a Muslim citizen caused great and serious unrest among the citizens. And the fourth crime is the violation of the integrity of an apartment, Article 56, the name of the street is the same, everything happened in the same street. The person -- the accused kicked in doors and entered apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And regarding this document, can we look at image 1264.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's the same register. We see the name of the person. Report filed by the 1st Military Police Battalion. Can we agree that this is the record of this file?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you two or three questions in conclusion. Sir, on the basis of the registers and the documents we've seen, it is evident that the crimes, although committed during the war and although they may have been qualified as crimes against humanity and a war crime, were actually qualified as regular crimes, rape, robbery, et cetera. Do you know the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents we've seen, each one of them specifies the crime for which proceedings are instituted. It is clearly specified in each case. Why proceedings were not instituted for war crimes, well that's mostly up to the prosecutor because it is the prosecutor who assigns a legal qualification to each offence. We see that in most cases the criminal report was filed by the military police, describing the reasons why the report is filed, and it is up to the prosecutor to qualify the crime. It is within his powers. In my opinion of the examples we've seen - and I repeat - we should not even go into why the prosecutor chose the particular qualifications that he did. It is his privilege. He has the right to qualify the crime in such a way as to have all the elements necessary for that conversation. I haven't commented and don't want to comment on why the prosecutor selected the particular qualifications. But as we've seen from the documents and as the penal code stipulates, both the federal and the republic penal code, injured parties had various options and legal remedies. In any case, a dissatisfied party could take various legal recourse: Appeal or start their own prosecution. All the legal recourse that existed in peacetime existed also in wartime and in the state of immediate threat of war. So nobody was derived of their legal recourse. Legal recourse existed throughout the state of war and the state of immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, over the past few days, we've discussed this subject and you presented us with a whole series of problems that the prosecution and the judiciary faced in their work. I would like to ask you something more.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, first, we should look at 1D 02006 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D 02016"].

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some more about the judiciary and the prosecution. It's a document that Branko Kvesic, the chief of the department on internal affairs, sends to the Capljina municipal HVO, and the subject is some important --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for document 1D 02006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2006. There it is. It's a report on the engagement of civilian police in carrying out combat tasks and the possibility of troop rotation. I'd like to see page 2 in both English and Croatian, the last paragraph but one, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: "It is common knowledge that in our area, the state of public law and order and the incidence of crime is very complex indeed," and then various crimes are enumerated, and it says it all false within the jurisdiction of the civilian police. We can skip one sentence, and it says: "With this report, we only wish to draw attention to the fact that so many of our policemen are currently engaged on other tasks that we do not have enough strength to undertake any serious work in the sphere of security." And the last sentence says: "All the above observations represent serious difficulties in our work, and we believe that they should be considered more seriously so that solutions be found in the most responsible manner."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show one more document and then ask my final question. P 05471.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It's from the chief of the military police department of the 29th September 1993. The subject is the same as in the previous document, and it says: "Request to reconsider the engagement of the military police units on front lines." The first paragraph states that due to the intensive and continuous engagement of military police units on front lines, the military police is unable to perform its regular work. And on page 2, there is a reference to increased incidence of terror and crime, and it is said that after being assigned the front lines, the military police are no longer able to perform even their regular work, let alone more complex interventions. Tell me, sir, were you familiar with this problem of the military and civilian police forces, that they were engaged on front lines and that that prevented them from their regular law enforcement work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this was sometimes discussed even at the sessions of the Croatian Defence Council. This burden and workload brought on by the war in terms of assigning military and civilian policemen to the front line caused fatigue, exhaustion. They were engaged first in the war with the Yugoslav People's Army and, later, with the Bosniak Muslim side. All this required the engagement of policemen on the battle-field, and it was often discussed how justified it was. And how possible it was to spare them from this, I don't know. So I don't think it's a question that I could give you a qualified or precise answer to, apart from saying that I know that the military police, and a little less frequently the civilian police, were assigned, indeed, to certain front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And my final question. We have seen all these documents that I showed you, and I showed them to you just by way of illustration because unfortunately we don't have enough time to show each and every case file from the prosecutor's office, either civilian or the military. And when we look at all the problems that you've been discussing over the past few days and in terms of the knowledge you had at the time, can you tell me whether there was an intention that you were aware of, either among the prosecution offices or the judiciary organs, to evade prosecution of crimes committed against ethnic Bosniaks and punishment of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know, both the civilian and the military police took measures to the best of their ability under the circumstances that they were in then, in order to discover who the perpetrators of crimes were and to file criminal complaints against them. We saw on the basis of these illustrations presented in court today that efforts were made to that end, and that ethnic Croats were charged for committing crimes against Bosniak or Muslim persons. It is, obvious on the basis of the examples shown. Also, in the proceedings before the prosecutor's offices and the courts of the HZ HB, it is obvious that there were proceedings of this kind with different outcomes. There were different outcomes, and there were decisions taken by courts. I do not wish to make any comments here in that respect because there is legal relief or legal recourse on the basis of the law, and no one was denied this kind of relief during the state of imminent threat of war or during the state of war. That is to say, there were no restrictions involved in terms of restricting human rights and the instruments safe-guarding these rights; rather, all the instruments for protecting human rights that existed in peacetime existed during the state of war as well. I'm not aware of any one of the prosecutors or judges being negligent in their duties or carrying them out unconscientiously or irresponsibly to the detriment of one of the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the basis of the cases we saw today, we saw that as prosecutors and as judges in these proceedings, prosecutors and judges who were ethnic Croats and ethnic Bosniaks participated. This is tellingly demonstrated in the cases we saw today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question, Witness, with respect to this last document, 5D 25006 [as interpreted], from the 2nd of September, 1993. It gives us an overview of the situation. And according to this document, the 1st Company of the military police is made up of 120 men. Apparently, 60 of these men are taking part in combat operations. There appear to be 120 soldiers on the ground. Out of these 120 soldiers, some of them must be on leave, sick, or others may be sleeping. In other words, there are very view military police members on the ground, very few of them. In this document, we have no information about the number of civilian police members, but we find that they are in combat zone operations as well. Considering the crime rate that was rising - and this has been demonstrated by all the documents shown by the Defence - we saw that crimes were committed in some cases by service men. As far as you were concerned as part of your duties at your level, was this problem considered, was it mentioned, and were measures taken; or was it impossible to take any measures considering the circumstances, considering the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous answer, perhaps I did not say clearly enough that I did know that units of the military police were used at war positions to a higher degree. I also know that civilian police units were used at the front line to a lesser degree; that is to say, that this was not something that was unknown. This was frequently the case as far as the military police is concerned; and as I already said, this question was discussed at HVO meetings several times and requests were being made to use them as little as possible. However, in view of the situation on the front line, or rather, during the war, it was such, and I imagine that the Court here did hear about the developments at the time. So, if I were to go back to that, I can say that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in effect started in September 1991; so not in April 1992, but rather on the 19th of September, 1991. So we had a situation in which individual municipalities would oppose perhaps the third- or fourth-largest military force in the world at the time. It is probably clear to the Court that that situation went on sometime until the summer of 1992; that is to say, this period of intensive conflict. Also, there was a lull from the summer of 1992 until the spring of 1993, when the conflict broke out between the Croats and the Bosniaks. Throughout this time - I believe that the Court is aware of that as well - the Croats in Central Bosnia were fully surrounded. There was a war breaking out throughout Herzegovina, if I can put it that way. It is certain that at that moment, it was more important - and I think that's quite understandable to the Court and to the Prosecutor I hope as well - to save human lives. Many people were being killed on a daily basis. As this administrative work was carried out - as I said, they were under the jurisdiction of the civilian and military police - the filing of criminal complaints was considered to be something that was not the primary or the most important objective at hand. The rest was considered to be more urgent and more important. The former could not be postponed; whereas, there was sufficient time for the latter; namely, that criminal complaints could be filed after some time had elapsed. However, if the front line were to fall, then there would be no possibility of filing any kind of criminal charges. So if the first thing had happened then the second could never have happened. Things were done the way they were done. However, as combat intensity went down, as we can see here, the head of the military police, or the head of the interior, submitted requests or proposals to the HVO to have certain units or certain number of men withdrawn from the front line and be given the duty to carry out their other tasks; that is to say to find perpetrators of crimes, file criminal complaints, and collect all possible information so that the prosecutor's offices could issue indictments and investigating judges investigate. At that point in time and now, I state that they carried out their work conscientiously to the degree possible at the time. There was never an intention or objective not to file criminal complaints against Croats, or rather, there were no intentional efforts made to jeopardize the members of the other ethnic group in any way. We see here that charges were being brought against Croats and terms of crimes that were committed against ethnic Bosniaks. There were also examples of investigations carried out after that and indictments issued. We see that prosecutors and judges were Bosniaks as well. I would not comment on judgements. They are judgements after all, and there was relieve for the protection of human rights as regulated by the then-legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was not reduced in any way by the decision made by the HZ HB. Your Honours, I don't know whether I've answered the question, but that was my understanding of it. I don't know whether it was put in this way, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are now going to move on to another Defence team. The Coric Defence has used 95 minutes in total. Next Defence team, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I won't have too many questions for this witness, and we are going to move within the time that you have granted to us. Actually, I'd like to say hello to Mr. Buntic, and to say that I'm going to deal with the subject that he dealt with Mr. Karnavas yesterday; and Mr. Buntic and I discussed the same subject a few days ago, if you remember, Mr. Buntic. I would just like to use three documents that are already exhibits. So with your leave, I would like to have these documents given to the witness as well as to the Trial Chamber. I would kindly ask the usher to assist me in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may use the time to put a question to you. You said you've spoken about this with the witness. Did you - as the jargon of the court is - proof him?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can put it that way. I informed Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Prlic's Defence, that I wished to see this witness. I thought that was my legitimate right. I think that last Thursday we had a brief meeting, about half an hour long, about some topics that I was interested in. The witness can confirm that, it's no secret, and this will be presented during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This raises in me the question whether your interrogation will not be direct then, rather than typically cross-examination; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will agree in part because I am going to move within the framework of Mr. Karnavas's direct examination. I'm not going beyond what happened in this courtroom over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, if I may, Your Honour, because I'm going to be going after the -- after we finish, we're going to be cross-examining. It's my understanding in our system, which is also applied here, that neither party, neither party, is prevented from meeting witnesses of the other party even prior to taking the stand. Nothing prevented me from meeting with Prosecution witnesses. In fact, on one occasion, I met with their expert. Of course, it was with their knowledge. And that didn't mean when I stood up I was doing direct examination. It has to go to the topic. So I would not want to say we have a fast and hard rule that if you meet with somebody else's witness, then that witness becomes your witness, hence you must do direct examination. So I just think that we need to clarify this point, and I would be more than happy to hear from the Prosecution. But in the 25 years that I've been practicing, I've often met with Prosecution witnesses and cross-examined them. It goes to the topic. And I'm sure Mr. Khan will put it more eloquently than I have, as he normally does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, not at all, but, nevertheless, the gracious remarks received with the sincerity that no doubt they were meant. Your Honour, there's no property, of course, in a witness. That's the starting point in assessing this matter. It's quite often the case that the -- it's quite often the case, as my learned friend Mr. Karnavas stated, that the Prosecution facilitate the Defence in various cases meeting with Prosecution witnesses prior to their testimony. Similarly, there's nothing to stop the Prosecution putting forward a request through Defence counsel to meet Defence witnesses. Of course, the matter for the -- the witness on both sides is whether or not they agree and consent to such an approach. But it cannot -- the simple fact of meeting cannot be said to be definitive as to whether or not questioning that follows is classed as cross-examination or examination-in-chief. Of course, the substance and content of the questioning will determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's exactly the Petkovic Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I had already thanked for the answer, Mr. Stewart; I think we've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, all I wished to do was associate the Petkovic Defence expressly with it, and we appreciate the thanks and we will take those, then, as coming to us as well for associating ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But sometimes for us it's a bit trying on the patience when several counsel, more or less, practically repeat one after the other the same points, and that's why I said we take the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I repeated nothing. When I do repeat things, Your Honour can then rebuke me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I go to the essential thing, so the essential things are the questions that are going to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buntic, have you received the documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know what they are about. First of all, it's the 46th Session of the government of 19 July 1993. At that session - document P 03560 - we see you were there, and Mr. Tadic, Darinko Tadic was there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: One of the issues at this cabinet session was initiated by this HVO Capljina, item 7.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that session, this working group was set up that was to visit Capljina: You, Mr. Tadic, and Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that session, based on the minutes, Mr. Pusic did not attend?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he was not even supposed to in view of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We can see from the introduction who was there, and his name is not included.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that the attendees do not include Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We also saw P 03565, the conclusions of the government about what this working group was to do and where it was to go. They were supposed to travel to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now I believe this trip - this may be a leading question - was on the same day, 19 July, because we see that the section session was on the 20th July, the morning; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. After this conclusion was adopted, Mr. Tadic, Mr. Pusic, and I visited Capljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know when you reached Capljina, who did you meet? Who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, we went to Capljina at the request of Capljina municipality that was addressed to the HVO. This group formed at this government session, immediately visited Capljina municipality, and we found there the deputy, I believe, of the president of Capljina municipality, Mr. Kordic. And he met us with the members of his office, and they familiarized us with the difficulties they were experiencing in making arrangements and providing accommodation for the large number of persons that found themselves in Capljina municipality, I believe from Gabela and Dretelj, and the very hard conditions there. They asked for assistance. So, in the municipality building, we talked to the chief of Capljina municipality, Mr. Kordic, and his deputies and assistants. I believe there were three or four deputies, each in charge of a specific area. So they told us about the difficulties they had in these two locations with accommodating the large number of persons in those locations. We spent an hour or perhaps two with them, and the very next day we submitted a report to the government which I suppose you can see from the minutes of the next session held the next day. And we suggested certain measures for that purpose; namely, that an urgent intervention is required because as the situation in Capljina was described to us, it was indeed very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: P 03573 is the 47th Session of the 20th July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you attached this document as well. It was held, therefore, the next day, and we see that the very next day we submitted a report. I can even read this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No need. Let me just ask you: You attended that session, but I don't see Mr. Pusic's name at the 47th Session?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the minutes, it seems to Mr. Pusic was not there, and I cannot recall him there. I believe he wasn't there; otherwise, he would have been recorded as present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now we came to the point you made a moment ago. This report, the way you told it I understood that the source for your report was the briefing you had in Capljina from Mr. Kordic and his people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We did not go to Gabela or Dretelj ourselves because I refused to go to Gabela and Dretelj. I did not believe myself competent to go there because, as we saw from the evidence presented yesterday, Dretelj was established as a municipal prison by virtue of a decision of the municipal council of Capljina municipality. And in keeping with the law on the enforcement of sentences, I as a representative of the department for justice and general administration, I had no powers or qualifications to enter such a facility. And at the end of the day, even if we said that I did have some authority, I did not have any powers in that sense. All that we learned, therefore, was from Mr. Kordic and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This trip that you made together, was it your first contact with Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me think for a moment. It's possible. It seems to me that I met Mr. Pusic perhaps six months prior. That was the first time we met when we discussed some technical issues like telephone lines and premises, and this was the second time. I don't think there were any more meetings between us in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buntic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I confess, I'm not quite satisfied with the explanations you have given for not looking at the accommodations, but maybe there is a linguistic problem. I read the task assigned to your group at the HVO meeting, the decision, to visit Capljina municipality and assess the condition of accommodation. Now, this was a task assigned to this group, and I find it difficult to accept an explanation which says "I was not competent to go and look at the accommodations." Was this not a basis that would have given you the task of looking at the accommodations in Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the letter sent by Capljina municipality, as I said earlier, the HVO made its decision based on the letter from Capljina municipality. The conclusion, as you see, of the HVO is adopted in relation to that letter from Capljina municipality. It is true that from the conclusion adopted by the government, it could arguably be understood what you understood. But I insist still that by going to a prison set up by the municipal council of Capljina with its own decision - and we saw that decision yesterday - the prison was set up as a municipal prison of Capljina municipality. By entering that prison, I would have perhaps led people to believe that I was in charge of what was going on in there, and I wasn't in charge and none of the three of us wanted to assume such responsibility. So we had no legal grounds, and I didn't want to take any action that could be understood that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, far from me, the thought of making it difficult for you, but I have in front of me documents; and as a Judge, I am duty-bound to ask certain questions. So there was a meeting on the 19th of July, 1993, at 10.00 in Mostar. Mr. Prlic presided over the meeting, and there are several participants including you. The agenda has several items, and the meeting will, of course, is to discuss these various items on the agenda. We can see the conclusions of the meeting. And in these conclusions under item 1 of the conclusions, page 4 in English, straight away it is mentioned -- the Geneva Conventions related to the treatment of prisoners of war are mentioned and that they call for a scrutiny of the detention conditions, which appear to be not satisfactory. Then the head of the department of justice, you are the one in charge, in coordination with the defence department and the department of the interior is supposed to inspect the new site and possibly envision transferring prisoners of war. A working group is set up. It's decided there, with you, Mr. Darinko Tadic and Mr. Pusic. And it is said in writing that you have to visit the Capljina municipality, and you have to inspect the detention conditions in proposed measures; in other words, at the 46th Session of the HVO of HZ HB, this problem was mentioned in discussed. Furthermore, it is also indicated under item 7 of the document that the minister for foreign affairs of the Republic of Croatia will have to be informed of all the problems, and that contacts will have to be established with the UNHCR. That means that the meeting looked into the issue of the prisoners of war. Earlier, you told us that you thought that Gabela and Dretelj were not within your field of competence. Would Gabela and Dretelj be within the remit of the Capljina municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as you know, in Gabela and Dretelj, were there prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know what was said that day when we visited Capljina municipality at a meeting attended by the head of the municipality and his various deputies who acquainted us with the difficulties they had. That also was contained in the letter they had sent to the authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They spoke about the overwhelming number of people. They sought assistance in food and in kind to be able to provide adequate conditions for the people held in those facilities. You correctly read the conclusions of the government and the reasons why the group was set up. Also, the same day this conclusion was adopted, we went to Capljina and completed all of our mission, except for the part which says to inspect in order to identify the conditions. But I have already stated my reasons for not going into those facilities, and I would do the same today. But we did collect all information from the head of municipality and the heads of his various services. We informed the government the very next day and proposed that immediate measures be taken so that at least half of the people in those facilities be transferred [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand properly, you answered part of my question. So based on the information you received on the spot, you thought it was not necessarily to go and visit the facilities because there were problems; therefore, you informed the government of the problems. Is that how to be understood? Is that the way we have to understand why you did not go to see with -- for yourself what you were told of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's one of the explanations. Because from the head of the municipality and his various deputies, we were able to get all the relevant information. That's one of the reasons, and the other reason I've stated already. The second is that I did not believe myself competent to enter those facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Still on these conclusions, the second paragraph on page 4 in the English translation says that: "If the accommodation conditions are not satisfactory," which was actually your conclusion, yourself, in coordination with the Ministry of the Interior and the defence department, "shall designate new sites and transfer prisoners of war." Now, the first question is: Did you do anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see at this session that was held on the very next day that -- well, the document is P 3573, the last document. Under A, Jadranko Prlic is for the municipality of Siroki Brijeg; B, Kresimir Zubak for the municipality of Grude and Posusje; C, Zoran Buntic for the municipality of Citluk; and, D, Martin Raguz for the municipality of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. On page 70, line 24, the gentleman indicated, according to Ms. Tomanovic, that the people in those facilities be let go, not transferred, as was translated. We're about to lose it right now. It's page 70, line 24, and perhaps we can pose the question again to Mr. Buntic because there is a major difference between half the people being let go versus them being transferred someplace else, which may have given rise to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, in relation to what my colleague Mr. Karnavas said, when I rose a few moments ago before Judge Trechsel put his question, I wanted to say precisely the very same thing in relation to the interpretation on line 24, page 70. So Mr. Karnavas's objection is fully correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I do not take it as an objection in the sense that I have quoted from the paper of course, but that doesn't mean that I was right because I cannot verify the translation of course. I think you have been now referring to what is stated on page 70, line 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. It was just a matter of correct translation, Your Honour, because the gentleman has indicated that he was suggesting that they let go; half of them he let go, not transferred. And, of course, it does make a -- it's a big distinction, at least in my mind. But we can pose the question to the gentleman, and he can answer or he can verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my suggestion would be to allow the witness to give his answer again and that we just take whatever interpretation that comes from the booth, recognising that there can be disagreements. But I think the witness should say it again so that we can get it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Witness, can you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the proposal of the group, this working group, was that due to the fact that there were too many people at these localities, one half be released straight away, half of these people, because there weren't proper conditions for keeping that many people in that number of square metres; and that the other half be moved to other localities, the remaining half, that is. On the next day, the HVO gave this duty to other persons, as I already mentioned a few moments ago, to have possibilities found in these other localities or municipalities for accommodating the remaining half. Your Honours, of course, I could not follow what the transcript was recording, but I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of course, that's all fine. The question, then, would be: Did you achieve anything in Citluk? Did you make efforts to find accommodations in Citluk which was assigned to you, as you have very correctly pointed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I made an effort, and I believe that all the other persons in charge made an effort, to find certain accommodation facilities in that sense that would be appropriate for the stay of these persons and conditions that would be in line with the conditions prescribed by the Geneva Conventions. However, none of the heads of the municipalities did not express a willingness to help the municipality of Capljina in that sense and to take a certain number of people in. It is correct, yes, I had these conversations and I believe that the others also talked to the representatives of other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you have perhaps already answered my last question which went to the role of the municipalities. Do I understand you correctly that you were saying implicitly that it was for the municipalities to agree or not to agree to offer a facility to accommodate prisoners, detained persons; and if a municipality would say, "We're not interested," that was it and the government had no possibility of acting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the areas of municipalities, the government, or rather, the HVO did not have any property that they owned. So if there was any property, it was owned by the municipalities. We have already said that in the territory of the other municipalities, apart from Mostar and Capljina, there was not a single facility that had earlier been owned by the SFRY or the Yugoslav Army so that the government or the HVO could have it at its disposal afterwards. The only facility of this nature -- or rather, the only facilities of such nature existed in Mostar barracks, two or three; and in Capljina where there were two barracks, one in Gabela and the other one was Dretelj. Well, you know, sometimes, sometimes, my mind seems to be blocked. So this was in the territory of Capljina, these barracks, and they had previously been owned by the JNA. In the territory of the other municipalities, there was no such facility under that kind of a regimen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have also personal experience of blocking of the mind now and then. A last question: Did the government have no possibility at all to expropriate property when it was needed for purposes of the whole of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed that issue as well, but probably had we done that we would have been prosecuted even more fiercely by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in session. I don't know who's the next counsel. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is showing that little binder of mine for this cross-examination. I asked the court deputy for it to be distributed to the Judges as soon as possible; however, I promise that I will finish with these documents within the time allotted to me. I will just explain that this document contain -- these binders contain documents that we will deal with today. There's also a big report that did not fit into the binder and another thing that will be useful to the Trial Chamber and to everyone in the courtroom is the Law on Criminal Procedure as a separate document, and I will be putting some questions to the witness about that. This Law on Criminal Procedure will be used by Ms. Alaburic after me. And I just wish to say that at the end of these subjects that are dealt with in the binder, at the very end I'm going to put some questions to the witness about some provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure that were referred to today in terms of the rights of injured parties, so that we could see that, indeed, the Law on Criminal Procedure does say all the things that the witness has told us; that is to say, the law that was then applied at the HZ HB. That is what I wish to say by way of introduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, Witness, on the first day of your testimony, you spoke about the situation in the area where you lived in 1991. You talked about the organization of the people to defend themselves from the aggression started by the JNA against Bosnia-Herzegovina and that part of the territory where you lived. You said that you did not have any weapons. You said -- you, rather, spoke about the Territorial Defence, and you said the JNA had taken away the weaponry of the Territorial Defence. And you mentioned that as for your first weapons for organizing the defence, that is to say, Croats and Muslims together in this area, you received these weapons from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To be more specific, you mentioned Mr. Bruno Stojic and Mr. Alija Delimustafic. For the record, can we first say specifically what position was held at that time, to the best of your recollection, in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Alija Delimustafic was minister of defence and his deputy was Mr. Bruno Stojic. What is stated is correct. I can only confirm that I said on the first day; namely, that from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we received 400 semiautomatic rifles that were new and unpacked. However, I remember that I did not say on the first day that later on, upon instructions of the same two persons, Delimustafic and Stojic, that is, we gave some of these weapons to the Bosniaks, the Muslims, for their needs, specifically for the area of Podvelezje. I think it involved 100 rifles. Perhaps ten or 15 days after we received them we handed them over. I cannot remember the name, but I know that this person introduced himself as the commander of the Crisis Staff for the area of Podvelezje. That is to the north-east of Mostar on the border between the municipalities of Mostar and Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to make short pauses between your answers and my questions. But, first of all, I would like us to correct two imprecisions that you provided in your answer, and they're recorded on page 77, lines 2, 3, and 4 -- or rather, 5 and 6. You said that Alija Delimustafic was minister of defence. That's a mistake. It's a slip of the tongue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purely a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell us, please, for the record, he was minister of what? I don't want to speak in your name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the entire remainder of the text that I uttered, and on the basis of everything I said by way of testimony until now, it is obvious that, to the best of my recollection, Mr. Alija Delimustafic was minister of the interior and his deputy was Mr. Bruno Stojic. Probably fatigue is taking its toll so I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to put a leading question to you, but I have the right to do that. If I tell you that Bruno Stojic was assistant minister for material technical affairs, rather than deputy minister, would you agree with me? This is also stated in the indictment. This is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. As I've already said, to the best of my recollection, but I do allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, we are going to go through some documents that confirm what you said -- rather, it is the first document in that black binder of mine, 2D 0033. And these are goods that were brought in and taken out. Would you briefly have a look at this, and I'm just going to refer to what is important. The date can be seen, the 20th of August, 1991. The first document you can see that it is incoming/outgoing of the republican secretariat of the interior. The number of this outgoing document states that this has to do with Hecklers, 15.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been instructed that it is 15 Hecklers, actually, and that these zeros are something that has to do with bookkeeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it is not 15.000, but it is 15 Hecklers. However, we are going to call a witness who dealt with these matters from a technical point of view, so he can explain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is obvious on the basis of the second item, because it would involve 400.000, but it was actually 400 semiautomatic rifles. So as you said it was probably 15 Hecklers and 400 semiautomatic rifles, as I've already said. So as regards both items, these three zeros are something that is a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to emphasize one more detail; namely, it's sent to the centre of security services Mostar. It was an organizational unit of the Ministry of the Interior in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We requested these rifles to arm the reserve force of the police. There was no other way to gets hold of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm not an arms dealer. I do not know what Heckler & Koch actually is. I suppose it's a pistol, but I may be wrong. Are they pistols, revolvers, the 9-millimetre weapon? Heckler & Koch 9-millimetre is the first item here. Is it a pistol, a handgun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This second abbreviation, "PAP," means semiautomatic rifle, so exactly what I said. Heckler & Koch is a sawn-off automatic rifle. It's not a revolver, it's not a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I was just about to ask the same question, but I was almost certain that all of us in the courtroom know that, because during the war, I, too, was in Sarajevo. I understand these acronyms as well as all names.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you look at the following document, please. The following document is an instruction or order for P 400. It's very precisely stated, 15 automatic rifles HK. And can you confirm that this is the signature of Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is Mr. Stojic's signature, and all the information that we received tells us with a great degree of certainty that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have one more document after that, and it's a new outgoing record, another 15 Hecklers; and the fourth document also sent to the security services centre Mostar. The following document speaks of 200 semiautomatic rifles; rounds, 31.500 rounds; four semiautomatic rifles; 20 Scorpion pistols; and 2.000 rounds 7.65-millimetres also sent to the security services centre Mostar. And the last document, 23rd September 1991, 20 semiautomatic rifles and 4.000 rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, the Chamber's Legal Officer is telling me that, yes, you are showing us some documents, but you need to give us the reference numbers. I suppose you're going to ask for document 2D 00033 to be tendered into evidence. But as for the individual documents, you need to give us their reference numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document on these four pages has been exhibited under the same number, 2D 0033 [as interpreted]. If you need page numbers, I see that apparently not. The Legal Officer seems to shake her head.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, can you confirm that in this period when both the Bosniak and Croat ethnic communities in the area where you lived in Herzegovina were both facing an aggression perpetrated by the JNA; and at the very outset, you were assisted specifically by Mr. Stojic, who was then-assistant minister in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. These documents attached here confirm all that I said on the first day of my evidence, and this seems to be material proof of what I said. I had only forgotten to mention that we also got ammunition together with these rifles. Perhaps I omitted it as a minor detail, but we did receive ammunition, 7.65. And I also know that out of all these weapons mentioned here, including the Scorpion pistol, five of these were sent also to Citluk municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, according to your testimony, all this was done in cooperation with the minister of the interior, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, who was a Bosniak; and all this was distributed and given to both Croats and Bosniaks; that is, to units including Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was all done in cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I mentioned what was done in Citluk, but it's obvious that from the documents that part of what Mr. Delimustafic and what Mr. Stojic agreed to and sent to the centre for security services was sent both to Citluk and to Mostar. It transpires from the document that the other 200 rifles probably ended up in Mostar, I suppose, for the requirements of the reserve force of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also mentioned Podvelezje. As far as that is concerned, you know for certain that one part of the weaponry was distributed in Podvelezje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will now broach a subject that was skimmed through in direct examination, and that is the establishment of the central military prison in Heliodrom, your participation and your knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put the documents in sequence as how I shall call them, and I hope there will be no problems with that. The first document is P 2 -- P 00292. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, have you found the documents?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a decree by Mr. Mate Boban, and I'll remind you in para 2 it governs the treatment of persons taken prisoner during armed conflict in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The decree was adopted on the 3rd of July, 1992, and para 2 says: "The Head of the Justice and Administration Department..." That is you; you occupied the position at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So: "The Head of the Justice and Administration Department, in cooperation with the Head of the Defence Department and the Head of the Department of the Interior, shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept, in accordance with the provisions of the aforementioned Convention," meaning the Geneva Convention. And in Article 3, we read: "The Defence Department shall administrate the facilities stipulated in Article 2 of this decree." So it follows from this decree that when following the procedure prescribed the location is determined, this location is run by the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I believe that in asking your question, you confused Article 2 and 3. That is Article 3, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at P 00452.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This has been shown to you before. This is from 3rd of September, 1992, signed by Mr. Stojic. And in the preamble, he invokes the previous decree. In Article 1, it says: "The central military prison is hereby established in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the Mostar-Jesenica location within the compound of the Heliodrom barracks." Mr. Mile Pusic is appointed warden; Mile Pusic from Krusevo, Mostar. I would like you to now tell us what you know about this. "At the proposal of the head of department for justice and administration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and in relation to the demonstrated need to separate the military prison from the district prison in Mostar, it having been established that the premises mentioned in para 1 of the decision meet all the prescribed requirements, I decided as stated above." In the course of your testimony, you also -- you already started to tell us something about the reasons why this decision was made. I'll just ask you to repeat this and expand, including those things that you did not have time to say.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Towards the end of the first day, I did give some of the reasons. A bit more was said on the subject yesterday; and as we can see from the statement of reasons, the statement of reasons confirms all that I said before. So after my conversation with the president of the higher court in Mostar about the state of affairs in the -- and the condition of the district prison in Mostar, the only facility of its kind in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the president of the court informed me that in the district investigating prison -- investigative prison in Mostar, in addition to convicted persons there are also prisoners of war. Immediately after, as we can see from the statement of reasons in this decision, I addressed a letter to the head of the defence department proposing a separation of prisoners of war from the convicts, so these two categories that were held together at the time in what was then the district investigative prison in Mostar. Immediately after that letter, the activities in this affair were managed by myself and - whether he was deputy of Mr. Stojic or an assistant for civilian affairs - Mr. Slobodan Bozic. Anyway, we established contact, and the only possibility we saw at that time was the Heliodrom barracks in Mostar. Mr. Lovric informed me of that; and as far as I know, work immediately started to adapt one building within the compound of the Heliodrom to adjust it to the requirements that a prison must meet. I'm not sure when the works were finished, but as you know they take time. And I believe that this prison was phased into operation with the proviso that at the initial stage, it held persons who were only subjected to disciplinary measures. After the building was fully adapted, already on the 3rd of December, this decision was passed. I'm saying maybe the body of the decision and the preamble are not entirely consistent. Maybe you can raise the issue of discrepancy. It is true that Mr. Bozic asked me concerning the warden whether I knew Mr. Pusic and whether I would object to appointing Mr. Pusic. I said I, indeed, knew Mr. Pusic, and I do not object. As far as I'm concerned, after this decision was passed, the matter was closed, because before the decision, the separation actually took place. So, after this decision in the district prison of Mostar, there remained only persons who were there pursuant to final court decisions..

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's deal with this more specifically now. At that time when you talked about this separation, who were the prisoners of war, of what ethnicity and from what war and from what conflict, what part of the conflict? And whose prisoners of war were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mainly had to do with prisoners of war who were members of the Yugoslav People's Army, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, were they taken prisoner in the conflict with the JNA that the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina took part in together? Can we conclude that these are prisoners that you had taken together, because that was the only location that you had in Mostar where they could be kept?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct. At that time, there was no other facility, no other possibility. It is correct, and now I have to make a correction. At that point in time, in Mostar, there was no Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, it is certain that, at the time, all the Muslims of Mostar operated within the HVO, or rather -- well, now, what was its name at the time? Later on, it was called the 5th Corps, but I think -- I beg your pardon, the 4th Corps. And, at that time, it was now -- was it a special independent battalion or company? I think it was called an independent battalion, and it operated within the HVO; but I'm saying this conditionally, these names. As far as my memory serves me, it was an independent battalion or something like that that operated within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's better for you to say that than me; although, it was established that it was the 1st Independent Battalion that was established beyond any doubt during the proceedings. However, I just wanted to set the record straight, and I think it is very important. So these prisoners of war, as you say, predominantly members of the JNA, were taken prisoner during the course of this conflict with the JNA in which you and the Bosniaks participated together, regardless of under whose command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and, yes, regardless of the name under which they operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just been cautioned that Mile Pusic was the head. Probably some other name was registered. It says Pusic in the document. I don't know. There was this intervention. I don't know what it pertains to, but at any rate I repeated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Further on, now we defined who the prisoners of war were. You said that it was necessary and that this was due to the need to separate the military prison in the district prison in Mostar. I'm interested in the following: Who were these prisoners? Were there civilians among them who were under the district prison, or rather, the regular courts and members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or rather, I beg your pardon, members of the HVO who were under the military judiciary? And was everybody together at the time? Was that separation supposed to be carried out, too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Everything that -- or rather, everyone that had been detained at that point in time was in that facility, as I already mentioned. I don't know whether it matters and whether it's relevant. The director of this -- or rather, the warden of this prison was appointed by the municipal HVO of Mostar. The person remained in that position for a considerable amount of time afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you just tell me what warden you're talking about of that prison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ricina Celovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's be specific, Ricina Celovina, because later on we're going to be using it further. So it's that prison, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, in your view, or rather, to the best of your knowledge because you participated, this decision was made in order to have a separation between civilian and military detainees and prisoners because at that time they were all in one location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask you to look at a document. We'll probably move faster, P 00352. The Court is aware of this document. I'm not going to mention the name of this witness. I know that it's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But we started talking about when work on the reconstruction of the facility had started. Please look at this document -- or rather, look at page 2 in the Croatian version and in the English version. This is a diary. I will tell you what is written there, the 1st of July, 1992, page 2. The notes pertain to the 1st of July, 1992. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Is it the handwritten document that I have?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to read it out to you. It says here: "The district prison in Mostar, Ricina number 27." That is the prison that we just talked about, right, that was supposed to be disburdened, or rather, a separation was supposed to be carried out, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I mean, I see from the address that it pertains to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says: "Morning briefing with the warden Pero Nikolic." Was Mr. Pero Nikolic the warden appointed by the municipal council that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now we are going to look at bullet point 4. "The warden informed those present that before the war, I was in charge, or rather, I was head of Radobolja business units, and he is a construction engineer otherwise, so he will spend most of his time at Heliodrom and oversee construction work to build or adapt a building that will be used as a military afterwards."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to look at the next page briefly, where we see a sketch of what is supposed to be the central military prison later on. We're going to look at the page after that too. I'm going to say for the record that I'm talking about ERN number 0354-0173 and page 0354-0174.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, do you remember whether on the 1st of July, as it says here when the adaptation of this building was being discussed, so we are talking about the 1st of July, 1993 [sic], Mr. Stojic was appointed head of the justice [sic] department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The year is 1992, yes. Sorry, slip of the tongue. There is a mistake in the transcript. I said 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speaker said "1993."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the Judge is intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You also said justice department, which is surprising.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to start all over again. I do apologise. I'll start all over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, do you know whether Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 1st of July, 1992, became head of the defence department of the HVO, or did that happen later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know, it happened after this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. So we can conclude that the work on the reconstruction of this building that would later become the central military prison started before Mr. Bruno Stojic became head of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, do you know at the time when this construction was taking place, did you know at all what the capacity of this area that was supposed to be the central military prison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about what I discussed at that point in time with other people. However, as far as I know, it had been envisaged, it was being said at that time, that the capacity would be between 500 to a maximum of 800 persons. That is what I had been told. I did not take part in the design of this facility. I'm not aware of any of that, and these sketches are unfamiliar to me. However, what was discussed was that the capacity would involve 500 to 800 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as you can remember from that period of time, was that actually the approximate number of prisoners of war, the persons who were supposed to be relocated at the time to that prison in Ricina, they were supposed to be relocated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that not all of them were in Ricina; but according to some of the information that the HVO had at the time, at that point there were about 500 prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would now like to ask you to look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to finish with this document, so then I'm going to continue dealing with the topic on Monday because I see the hour. P 00420 is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will explain what this is about because it starts with page 29, this document. This is a Prosecution document on the 65 -- or rather, I beg your pardon. The bulletin of the military police numbers 2 and 3 for July and August, that's what it's called on the Prosecution list, 1992. The date is the 31st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will only deal with page 59 in the Croatian and English versions, and I'm going to ask only what I show to the witness to be admitted into evidence. I'm saying this, lest there be any objections in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On page 59, Mr. Buntic, we see exactly what we have been discussing; that is to say, on the basis of this bulletin dated the 31st of August, 1992, it says: "Military investigative detention facilities were formed out of necessity on premises unsuitable for taking in the necessary number of prisoners of war, or rather, prisoners. Also, arrangements in the prison are such that it's very difficult to ensure a continuous, professional, and high-quality investigative procedure. For that reason, the necessity of establishing a central military prison was unavoidable, and this was done at the barracks in the Mostar Heliodrom. "We believe that it must be made operational as soon as possible so that military and civilian prisons in Mostar would be separated and in order to redress the weaknesses mentioned. In keeping with this, the military police administration and the management team of the Mostar prison are carrying out all necessary preparations for the central military prison to begin functioning. It will be able to take in up to 800 prisoners of war or military prisoners." Finally, Mr. Buntic, this document confirms what you said; namely, that the original intention was that the capacity should be up to 800 persons at maximum and that the building was being adapted with that in mind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, what I stated earlier on is shown; namely, that the planned capacity was between 500 and 800 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to end. It's quarter to 2.00. There's another sitting. I'm sitting also in another case. As you know, we shall re-convene on Monday. You will start at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
